description: The regional compute pact between France, Germany, and Poland fails to meet integration deadlines due to unresolved legal disputes over data sovereignty and operational control. Mutual distrust over access protocols and fear of asymmetric dependency stall joint procurement and red-team coordination, leaving the European Red-Team Grid under-resourced and fragmented. This delay undermines confidence in EU-wide compute resilience and exposes the limits of intergovernmental cooperation under pressure.

A leaked internal report from a major AI laboratory reveals that safety testing was systematically deprioritized during the last training run to meet a release deadline, despite known anomalies. The disclosure triggers a transatlantic outcry, with EU regulators demanding audits and whistleblower protections. Public and technical communities alike begin to frame the current safety deficit not as an unavoidable trade-off but as a consequence of institutional negligence, accelerating calls for binding oversight mechanisms.

A wave of public-sector resignations in AI oversight bodies, including EASA and national regulators, follows the leaked lab report and perceived institutional failure. The resignations are framed as a protest against political interference and underfunding, accelerating the talent drain already noted in emergent_ai_talent_drain. This further degrades the EU’s capacity to respond to the capability leap.

A coalition of Nordic and Benelux states, frustrated by the stalled regional compute pact, begins informal coordination on red-teaming and model evaluation using existing bilateral agreements. This nascent network operates outside EU structures but shares intelligence and testing results, creating a shadow governance layer. It reflects growing fragmentation in EU AI policy.
